Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Arthur, a seasoned politician of sixty-eight years, had always prided himself on his composure and sharp intellect. However, the world shifted beneath his feet six months ago, after the accident. He had been on his way home from a late-night council meeting, navigating the familiar suburban roads when, without warning, a vehicle swerved into his lane. The crash was a blur of screeching metal and shattering glass, a few indelible snapshots burned into his mind: the blinding flash of headlights, the sickening lurch, and the sudden, crushing impact. When the memory returned, it wasn't just a mental image; he would feel a sharp, phantom pain in his ribs and his left leg, precisely where the dashboard had pinned him. If asked to recount the event, Arthur would start strong, but inevitably lose his thread mid-sentence, the narrative dissolving into fragmented images and sensations he couldn't quite articulate.

In the weeks and months that followed, Arthur found himself increasingly consumed by a relentless inner monologue. He dwelled obsessively on what he believed he had done wrong, repeatedly blaming himself for the collision. He was certain the accident had happened because of the sort of person he was—perhaps too trusting, or not vigilant enough, a flaw he now felt was deeply ingrained in his character. This conviction left him feeling perpetually exposed; he imagined that others, particularly his constituents and colleagues, could somehow see his perceived failing just by looking at him, a vulnerability he desperately tried to conceal. He felt he had to be on guard all the time, constantly scanning his environment for any sign of danger.

This hypervigilance permeated every aspect of his life. Even at home, in the quiet of the night, he would frequently wake with a jolt, his heart pounding, compelled to check that he and his wife were safe. An unusual silence, once a welcome respite, now made him feel as if something dangerous was about to happen, sending a prickle of anxiety up his spine. His ability to concentrate, once his greatest asset in his political career, had dwindled; during council debates or when reviewing policy documents, his mind would wander, unable to hold onto complex information.

The world outside his home became a minefield of triggers. The faint smell of alcohol, encountered at a campaign reception or even just walking past a restaurant, would instantly transport him back to the acrid scent he remembered from the other driver's breath at the crash scene, tightening his chest. Seeing images of cars hit by accidents, whether on the news or just a damaged vehicle by the roadside, would flood him with dread. Even a general feeling of physical discomfort, a slight ache or an unfamiliar sensation, would trigger a wave of unease, a premonition of impending disaster.

The most significant change, however, was his complete avoidance of driving or being a passenger in a vehicle. He simply couldn't bring himself to get into a car. This presented immense challenges for a politician whose role demanded constant travel to meetings, community events, and fundraisers across the district. His wife, Maria, had been driving him everywhere, but even then, Arthur would sit rigid in the passenger seat, his knuckles white on the door handle, scanning the road with an intensity that left him exhausted. He had begun to decline invitations to events that were too far or too complex to navigate without a driver, explaining away his absence with vague excuses. This had started to impact his visibility in the community and created a growing distance from his usual routines. The consequences were accumulating: missed opportunities, a growing reliance on his wife, and a pervasive sense that his career, and indeed his life, was shrinking. It was this creeping constriction, the realization that he was losing control over his own life and his capacity to serve, that finally led Arthur to seek help, desperately hoping to reclaim the man he once was.
